lesson_title: What Really Runs Out in a Battery
hook_text: Your torch goes dim during load shedding. Did the battery run out of electricity? Not exactly.
clip_script: Load shedding hits, you grab a torch, and it lights. Inside: two cells, a switch, a bulb and some metal strips, a tiny energy system. Close the switch and you complete a loop. The cells push charges around it. The charges pick up energy in the cells, drop it off in the bulb as light and heat, and come back for more, round and round like a bicycle chain. Make a gap anywhere and everything stops. So when the torch goes dim, did it run out of charges? No. The same charges are still there. What ran out is the energy stored in the chemicals inside the cells. And most of the energy in an old-style bulb never even becomes light: about ninety-five percent turns into heat. That is why LED bulbs, which waste far less, are the smart choice.
visual_style: A whiteboard torch cut open, with dots circulating round the loop picking up energy at the cells and releasing it as light at the bulb, then a Sankey arrow splitting into light and heat.
pacing: A relatable opening, a clear loop animation, then a punchy reveal.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and trace the energy in a circuit.
